net orders: Orders received minus cancellations over a period. The cleanest measure of real demand for an aircraft maker.
A320neo: Airbus's best-selling single-aisle jet family. 'neo' = new engine option, roughly 15-20% less fuel burn than the original A320.
narrowbody: A single-aisle airliner (e.g. A320, 737) used mostly on short and medium routes.
widebody: A twin-aisle airliner (e.g. A350, 787) used mostly on long-haul routes.
MRO: Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul: the business of keeping aircraft and engines airworthy. A large, steady aftermarket revenue pool.
aftermarket: Revenue earned after a product is sold: spare parts, repairs and services. For engine makers it is often more profitable than selling the engine.
OEM: Original Equipment Manufacturer: the company that designs and builds the product (Airbus, Boeing, GE, Rolls-Royce), as opposed to third-party suppliers.
turbofan: The jet engine type on almost every airliner: a large front fan pushes most air around the core, which makes it quieter and more fuel efficient.
certification: Regulator approval (FAA, EASA, Rosaviatsia...) proving an aircraft type is safe. Requires hundreds of test flights; delays here delay deliveries.
air taxi: A small, usually electric aircraft (eVTOL) meant to carry a few passengers across a city, taking off and landing vertically.
eVTOL: electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing aircraft, the technology behind most planned air taxis.
trade secret: Confidential business information (designs, processes) protected by law. Misusing a rival's trade secrets can lead to large damages.
Series D: A fourth major round of venture funding. By this stage investors expect a clear path to revenue; failing to close one can threaten the company.
hydrogen-electric: A powertrain where hydrogen feeds a fuel cell that makes electricity for electric motors, emitting only water.
slots: Permission to take off or land at a congested airport at a specific time. At airports like LaGuardia they are scarce and very valuable.
antitrust: Competition law. Regulators review deals to make sure they do not give one company too much market power.
lessor: A company that owns aircraft and rents them to airlines. Lessors own around half of the world's airliner fleet.
damp-lease: Leasing an aircraft with part of the crew (usually pilots) included; between a dry lease (aircraft only) and a wet lease (aircraft, crew, maintenance, insurance).
profit outlook: Also called guidance: the earnings range a company tells investors to expect. Cutting it usually moves the share price.
jet fuel: Kerosene-based fuel. Typically 25-30% of an airline's costs, so oil price shocks hit airline profits quickly.
Federal Reserve: The US central bank. It sets interest rates to manage inflation and employment; its independence from the president is a long-standing norm.
net zero: Cutting greenhouse-gas emissions as far as possible and balancing the rest with removals, so the total added to the atmosphere is zero.
COP17: The 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, where governments negotiate nature-protection targets.
desalination: Removing salt from seawater or brackish water to make drinking water. Reliable but energy-hungry and expensive to build.
lithium: The key metal in rechargeable batteries for EVs and electronics. Extracting it often uses large amounts of water.
CBO: Congressional Budget Office: a non-partisan US agency that estimates the costs of policies for Congress.
deepfake: AI-generated video, image or audio that convincingly imitates a real person.
peer review: Checking of a scientific paper by independent experts before publication; the main quality filter in science.
robotaxi: A driverless taxi service (e.g. Waymo, Tesla), operating without a human safety driver.
green card: US lawful permanent residency, allowing someone to live and work in the US indefinitely.
visa programme: Here, a US work-visa scheme that lets employers hire foreign skilled workers.
Starlink: SpaceX's satellite internet network, now also sold to airlines for in-flight wi-fi.
spectrum: Radio frequencies governments license to telecom and satellite operators.
impairment: A write-down: the company admits an asset is worth less than it paid, and books the difference as a loss.
OPT: Optional Practical Training: lets international students work in the US for one to three years after graduating.
H-1B: The main US visa for skilled foreign workers, mostly used by tech companies.
CADE: Brazil's competition regulator, which reviews mergers and stakes for antitrust risk.
Chapter 11: US bankruptcy process that lets a company keep operating while it restructures its debts.
earnings per share: Profit divided by the number of shares. The headline number investors use to judge a company's results.
New Keynesian: The mainstream economic model behind modern central banking: prices adjust slowly, so interest rates and expectations can steady the economy.
monetary policy: What a central bank does with interest rates and money supply to control inflation and support jobs.
G7: Group of Seven large advanced economies: US, Japan, Germany, UK, France, Italy, Canada.
IMF: International Monetary Fund: lends to countries in trouble and publishes widely watched economic forecasts.
MQ-9 Reaper: A large US military drone used for surveillance and strikes.
Kunming-Montreal: The 2022 global biodiversity agreement with 23 targets for 2030, including protecting 30% of land and sea.
acre-feet: A US water unit: enough to cover one acre one foot deep, about 1.23 million litres.
pneumonic plague: The lung form of plague. It can spread person to person, but is treatable with antibiotics if caught early.
preprint: A research paper shared publicly before peer review.
NHTSA: The US road safety regulator, which collects crash data on self-driving cars.
Sentencing Commission: A US agency that writes the guidelines federal judges use to set prison sentences.
deference: When courts accept a government agency's interpretation of an unclear rule instead of deciding it themselves.
Strait of Hormuz: The narrow sea lane out of the Persian Gulf; about a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through it.
transition businesses: An energy company's low-carbon divisions: renewables, hydrogen, EV charging and similar.
Treasury yield: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow. When it rises, mortgages and company loans get more expensive too.
Brent: The main global benchmark price for crude oil.
earnings season: The few weeks each quarter when most big companies report their results.
correction: A fall of 10% or more in a stock index from its recent peak.
